Chapter 8: Raising Indistractable Children—Teaching Focus and Self-Regulation.
You know, distraction isn’t just something adults struggle with. Kids and teenagers are right there with us, facing their own battles to stay focused—especially with all the digital devices and social pressures around them.
Helping young people become indistractable isn’t really about laying down strict rules.
It’s about building the skills for self-regulation and intentional choices.
The very first step? Modeling what a healthy relationship with technology looks like.
Kids watch what we do, way more than what we say. So, if you put your phone away during dinner, or really listen when they talk, you’re showing them what mindful device use looks like.
Try narrating those choices out loud—something simple, like, “I’m putting my phone away so I can listen.”
That little moment? It makes a big impact.
Invite your kids to help set up family guidelines for using devices, and show them how technology can be a helpful tool—not just an easy way to escape when things get tough.
But there’s more. It’s just as important to help kids recognize their own internal triggers. So, when a child reaches for a device because they’re bored or upset, use it as a chance to talk about what’s really going on inside.
Ask open questions, like “What are you feeling right now?” Or brainstorm together: “What else could you do when you feel bored?”
Encouraging breaks, a little movement, or even a quick walk can help them reset their attention in a healthier way.
Of course, having some boundaries with devices is helpful, but here’s the key—stay flexible. Instead of blanket bans, try creating family agreements about when and how devices are used.
Maybe you all agree to make mealtimes or bedtime tech-free.
Check in as a family now and then, and update those agreements as life changes.
The focus isn’t just on what you’re restricting, but on building real connections and shared activities.
At the end of the day, teaching kids to notice their triggers, manage discomfort, and make intentional choices gives them lifelong skills for focus.
This is how you extend the indistractable framework through your whole family—showing that attention isn’t just a personal value, but something you all stand for together.
